source_read: PDF, printed pp. 1450–1461 (all 12 pages; Tables 1–4 and Figures 1–3 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; born-digital text layer agreed with the rendered pages)

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of this source; the claim is more cautious than the authors, whose abstract (p. 1450) concludes that the semantic-memory deficit is reversible and the episodic deficit long-lasting. Minor: 'story recall ... lower at both sessions' is the authors' description for immediate recall only; for delayed recall they report only an overall group effect, and Fig. 3b shows the gap at follow-up narrowing because the controls' recall fell (about 9.7 to 8.2) while the ketamine group stayed about 7.2 to 7.5. 'Cut down' is true of days of use, not of amount per occasion, which rose (0.31 to 0.44 g, SD 0.97).
claims.note: Every 2004a number in the statement and magnitude is on the page. Editors' calculation '18 of the 57': I get 57 too (19 original ketamine participants who took part plus the 38 of the original ketamine group who could not be contacted, pp. 1452 and 1459; the paper itself prints only 76 original participants). F and t values all reproduce their P values (F(1,26) = 5.19 gives P = 0.031; t = 2.42 gives P = 0.023). The correlation r = 0.712 (P < 0.002) fits n = 18 (P = 0.0009), but the paper gives neither the n nor how 'change in ketamine use' was signed (change is defined only for category fluency, follow-up minus baseline), so the direction rests on the authors' wording; the same gain correlated as strongly with time since last use (r = 0.723), so reduction and time since use cannot be separated. The 10 controls can only have come from Curran & Morgan (2000), because Curran & Monaghan (2001) had no ketamine-free group, and the paper does not say how many of the 18 came from each earlier study; the authors note that participants from the 2001 study had poorer attention at baseline (p. 1458), so the baseline comparison differs from both original comparisons. (Reader's own locator for the speed-of-comprehension anchor corrected from '1st and 2nd paragraphs' to '1st paragraph' on re-checking the rendered page during step 2: the paragraph runs across both columns.)

anchors.extracted: Independent-group longitudinal design; baseline = the day-3 (drug-free) session of two earlier studies (Curran & Morgan 2000; Curran & Monaghan 2001), retested 3 to 4 years later. 33 of the original 76 could be contacted; 31 took part, including 19 original ketamine participants; 1 who had developed schizophrenia and 2 controls who had started ketamine were excluded, leaving 18 ketamine and 10 polydrug controls.

None had escalated or kept the same level of use; all reported few problems cutting down. 38 members of the original ketamine group could not be contacted and may have continued use; no continuing-use group; other factors may have led this sample to cut down; pre-existing differences cannot be ruled out without prospective studies. (19 + 38 = 57 original ketamine participants, reader's calculation, same as the editors'.)

Ketamine group cut its frequency of use by an average of 88.3% (mean of individual reductions; the ratio of the group means gives 75%); 8 had not used for over 6 months; mean 1.61 (SD 3.19) days a month at follow-up against 6.45 (8.13) at baseline; self-reported amount per occasion rose from 0.31 (0.25) to 0.44 (0.97) g.

anchors.locator: Results › Cognitive tasks › Semantic memory, 1st paragraph (category generation); Fig. 1 (p. 1455)
anchors.extracted: Category fluency: group x time F(1,26) = 5.19, P = 0.032; time F(1,26) = 7.50, P = 0.011; lower in the ketamine group on day 3 (t printed with df 1,27 = 2.42, P = 0.023), no difference at follow-up. Fig. 1 (reader's reading): about 16.0 vs 20.8 exemplars at baseline, about 20.2 vs 21.2 at follow-up. Perseverative errors higher in the ketamine group at both sessions, F(1,26) = 6.13, P = 0.02 (Table 3: 1.94 vs 0.5; 1.29 vs 0.4).

Change in category fluency (follow-up minus baseline) correlated with change in ketamine use, r = 0.712, P < 0.002, and with time since last ketamine use, r = 0.723, P < 0.002; n and the sign convention for change in use not stated (Method says within-group correlations were run). Digit-cancellation time did not correlate with recall.

anchors.locator: Results › Speed of comprehension task, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2; Table 3
anchors.extracted: Sentences judged: main effect of group F(1,26) = 8.73, P = 0.007, fewer in the ketamine group at both sessions; Fig. 2 (reader's reading) about 62 vs 86 at baseline and about 73 vs 83.5 at follow-up. Errors: interaction F(1,26) = 4.35, P = 0.047, difference on day 3 only, errors at floor at follow-up (1.06 vs 0.2; 0.38 vs 0.4).

anchors.locator: Results › Episodic memory, 1st paragraph; Digit cancellation, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3
anchors.extracted: Immediate prose recall: group F(1,26) = 4.36, P = 0.047, controls better on both occasions (Fig. 3a about 7.9 vs 10.3 and 7.5 vs 9.0). Delayed: group F(1,26) = 4.43, P = 0.045, worse overall in the ketamine group, with a visible fall in controls (Fig. 3b about 7.2 vs 9.7 and 7.5 vs 8.2); no interaction reported for either. Digit cancellation: group F(1,26) = 7.09, P = 0.013, no interaction or time effect; 66.01 (14.12) and 65.32 (11.34) s vs 54.60 (7.82) and 55.97 (8.74) s; errors did not differ.
Prose recall at follow-up similar to baseline; with groups matched on drug use, the authors say the deficit could reflect either pre-existing differences or ketamine use.

Authors conclude that semantic-memory impairments are reversible on marked reduction of use and that episodic (and possibly attentional) impairments appear long-lasting: a firmer reading than the design (18 vs 10, 38 of 57 lost, no continuing-use group, self-reported use) allows, and the opposite of the claim's 'insufficient to say'.

claims.overstatement: None for this source. The SSQ is a state questionnaire (p. 1453) that the authors say may still tap traits (p. 1459); 'psychosis-like (schizotypal)' is a fair plain label.
claims.note: All 2004a numbers check against Table 4 (p. 1455) and Table 1 (p. 1454). Depression (HADS) was measured only at follow-up, as a rating of the past week, so it is a single-session difference, not a change. The printed test for it does not hold up: U = 55.5 for groups of 18 and 10 gives two-tailed p of about 0.10 (one-tailed about 0.05), not the printed P < 0.031; a t-test on the printed means and SDs gives p of about 0.04 (Welch about 0.02). The other U tests on p. 1456 reproduce their P values with these group sizes, and the cannabis-years test (U = 46.5, printed P = 0.052) gives about 0.04. One internal inconsistency: p. 1452 says the person who developed schizophrenia was excluded before the 18 were formed, but p. 1459 says it was one of the sample of 18; the claim follows p. 1452.

anchors.locator: Table 4 (SSQ total, ADSS total rows); p. 1456 Results › Subjective measures › Schizotypal Symptomatology Questionnaire and Adapted Dissociative States Scale, 1st paragraphs
anchors.extracted: SSQ: 51.5 (21.28) vs 24.8 (8.16) at baseline (day 3 after use), 18.67 (17.05) vs 4.0 (4.06) at follow-up; group F(1,26) = 15.32, P = 0.001; day F(1,26) = 59.25, P < 0.001; no interaction, so scores fell in both groups and stayed higher in the ketamine group. ADSS: 10.11 (15.38) vs 5.44 (5.85), and 3.24 (4.53) vs 0.80 (1.54); only time F(1,26) = 5.93, P = 0.022 (fall in both groups), no group difference.

At follow-up only: HADS depression 5.27 (4.32) in the ketamine group vs 2.00 (2.45) in controls, U = 55.5, P < 0.031 as printed (reader's recalculation for 18 vs 10: two-tailed p about 0.10); HADS anxiety 7.89 vs 6.63, no difference.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: No correlation between schizotypal symptoms and ketamine use; scale adapted to index state schizotypy but may tap traits; pre-existing differences or chronic effects cannot be told apart. The ketamine group was not within a clinical range of depression; HADS could not be compared with baseline (not reported in the 2001 study; the 2000 participants had not differed from controls on depression).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high overall, driven by selection (18 of 57 original ketamine participants, all of whom had cut down, and 38 uncontacted who may have kept using); the domain judgments match what the paper reports.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract states reversibility and persistence that the design cannot separate from pre-existing differences, practice or selection; the card's point that 10 of the 18 had used within 6 months, so persistence after cessation is not shown, is correct (p. 1454).

missed: Depression test (p. 1454, Table 1 and Results › Demographics): U = 55.5 for groups of 18 and 10 gives two-tailed p of about 0.10 (one-tailed about 0.05), not the printed P < 0.031; a t-test on the printed means and SDs gives about 0.04 (Welch about 0.02). The cannabis-years test, U = 46.5 printed as a trend (P = 0.052), gives about 0.04. The three subjective-effects U tests on p. 1456 do reproduce their P values with these group sizes. Suggest adding as a reporting issue: the follow-up depression difference is less secure than printed.

Digit cancellation (p. 1458, Discussion › Attention and working memory, 1st paragraph): the ketamine group mixes participants from two earlier studies, and the authors say those from Curran & Monaghan (2001) already had poorer attention at baseline and that the persisting difference was surprising because the 2000 study had found none. The controls all come from the 2000 study and the split of the 18 is not given, so the slower times at both sessions may partly reflect sample composition. The card's comparison field names the control source, but no finding draws this consequence.
